title: Agencies Step Up After Congress Fails to Act
summary: The Senate blocked the CLARITY Act from advancing last week, and within days both the SEC and the CFTC moved to write the market structure rules Congress didn't.

## Key Takeaways


-


Agencies move where Congress didn't. Days after the Senate blocked the CLARITY Act, the SEC and CFTC each issued relief of their own to fill the gap Congress left.


-


A trading pilot for tokenized equities. The SEC's order is a temporary exemptive order clearing permissioned on-chain trading of tokenized equities, work that predates the vote by over a year but lands with useful timing.


-


Narrower than the headline suggests. The SEC's two five-year exemptions cover only real, issuer-linked shares, arrive with 30-plus disclosure conditions, and are explicitly framed as an interim pilot pending further rulemaking.


-


The CFTC follows with its own fix. The same day the SEC's order took effect, the CFTC's Market Participants Division expanded an existing no-action position from a single beneficiary to any similarly situated software provider offering passive access to regulated derivatives markets.


-


An administrative patch, not a permanent fix. Both actions are revocable at their issuing agency's discretion and apply only until formal rulemaking or legislation catches up, leaving firms to navigate two separate, uncoordinated regimes until Congress passes something comprehensive.


## Regulatory Agencies Waste No Time Following Failed CLARITY Advancement in Writing its Own Rules


The Senate blocked the CLARITY Act from advancing last week, and within days both the SEC and the CFTC moved to write the market structure rules Congress didn't. The SEC issued a temporary conditional exemption clearing a path for permissioned on-chain trading of tokenized U.S. equities. The CFTC's Market Participants Division expanded an existing no-action position to cover any software provider offering passive access to its regulated derivatives markets. The timing invites an obvious read. Congress failed to write digital asset market structure rules, so both Commissions are writing their own.


## The SEC Moves First


The groundwork for the SEC action order predates the CLARITY Act vote by over a year. The SEC's Crypto Task Force was established back in January 2025, and in July 2025 Chairman Atkins launched "Project Crypto" as a Commission-wide modernization initiative. This order is unlikely to be an improvised reaction to the Senate's vote, but the timing is probably opportunistic rather than causal. The Commission didn't need the CLARITY Act to fail to have authority here, exemptive relief has always been available to it independent of any legislative outcome. What the failed vote does is hand the SEC a useful juxtaposition; an agency capable of writing its own rules within days, set against a legislature that couldn't move at all.


## The Exemption Is Narrower Than the Headline Suggests


The order grants two distinct exemptions, both temporary and both running five years, from September 17, 2026 to September 17, 2031. The first exempts "Tokenized Securities Venues," or TSVs, from the Exchange Act's definition of "exchange." This exemption allows them to operate AMM (Automated Market Maker) liquidity pools for permissioned trading of tokenized equities without registering as a national securities exchange or ATS. The second exempts certain liquidity providers, termed "Covered Firms," from the definition of "dealer" so long as their activity is confined to supplying liquidity within a TSV's AMM pools using their own capital.


What can actually trade is narrower than "tokenized securities" as a category might suggest. The order applies specifically to "Tokenized NMS (National Market System) Stock," meaning a security tokenized by or on behalf of the issuer, or tokenized by an unaffiliated third party, of an underlying NMS stock. It explicitly excludes tokenized linked securities and tokenized security-based swaps, the synthetic-exposure wrappers that would have been the more obvious vehicle for standing up crypto-native exposure to equities without touching the underlying share register. The Commission wants tokenized claims on real shares carrying real shareholder rights, not derivatives dressed up as tokens.


Exemptions arrive with a long list of conditions, thirty-plus disclosure items in the required public notice alone. The order covers everything from governance structure to MEV mitigation to circuit breaker procedures. That's the tell that this is a supervised pilot with an exit ramp back to formal rulemaking, not a deregulatory green light. The Commission says as much directly, framing the order as an interim measure "while the Commission considers the need for future rulemaking." It closes with ten separate comment questions soliciting feedback on whether any of this should become permanent.


## A Lighter Rulebook, But a Small Sandbox


There's a reasonable case that this order threatens traditional stock exchanges. TSVs are exempt from several rules exchanges normally have to follow. For example, guaranteeing traders get the best available price or disseminating live quotes, since these platforms price trades using an automated formula based on the ratio of assets in a pool rather than by referencing outside markets. That's a much lighter compliance burden, and lighter rules usually pull in trading volume.


But the caps built into the order keep that threat small. The most liquid stocks, think S&P 500 companies, can only be tokenized up to 75 different stocks per venue, and total tokenized trading in any one stock can't exceed a quarter of a percent of its normal daily trading volume. Less liquid stocks get more room, up to 250 symbols and 2.5% of volume, but breach either limit twice and the venue has to stop trading that stock for three months. A quarter of a percent of daily volume in the country's biggest, most-traded stocks just isn't enough to threaten a real securities exchange.


There's also a safeguard that doesn't exist anywhere else in the market: the company behind a stock can object to having its shares tokenized, and if it does, that venue simply can't offer it. No stock exchange today gives companies that kind of veto. Combined with a rule barring these venues from letting traders borrow money to trade, the picture that emerges isn't a backdoor around exchange rules. It looks like regulators are building a contained testing ground small enough to watch closely without worrying it spills into the main market.


## The Tradable Universe Is Equities Paired with Crypto, Not Crypto Trading Freely


A Tokenized NMS Stock on a TSV can only trade in one of three pairs, another Tokenized NMS Stock, a GENIUS Act stablecoin, or a tokenized money market fund. There's no primary issuance on a TSV, and every Tokenized NMS Stock must carry the same economic and voting rights as the underlying share, including proxy materials at no cost to holders.


In practice, the "crypto asset" half of every trade is constrained to instruments the Commission has already blessed elsewhere, like stablecoins for settlement or money market fund tokens for cash management. It is not an open door to pairing equities against whatever token has liquidity. Notably, the order's own description of AMM mechanics casually cites the constant-product formula (x*y=k), a small but real sign of how far DeFi vocabulary has crept into a release that also spends pages on OFAC compliance and recordkeeping.


What this amounts to is permissioned, stablecoin-settled trading of tokenized equities inside a volume-capped sandbox, not a bridge to the broader digital asset market. That’s not quite the crypto market bonanza the industry might want, but it’s a step in the right direction.


## The CFTC Follows With a Broader No-Action Position of Its Own


The CFTC's Market Participants Division didn't wait long either. On September 17, 2026, the same day the SEC's exemptive order took effect, the CFTC released an interpretive letter. The letter expanded a no-action position first granted six months earlier to a single company into blanket relief for an entire category of firms. The mechanics are different from the SEC's order, but the instinct is the same: rather than wait on Congress, the regulator is reaching for the tools already on its own shelf.


The starting point was a letter issued in March 2026 to Phantom Technologies, a developer of self-custodial crypto wallet software that wanted to let its users route orders directly into CFTC-regulated derivatives markets. The CFTC gave Phantom a no-action position meaning the Division would not recommend enforcement against Phantom for failing to register as an introducing broker, or against its personnel for failing to register as associated persons, so long as Phantom stuck to a defined set of "Proposed Activities."


## Same Instinct, a Different Tool


Where the SEC reached for exemptive relief under the securities laws to build something close to a new market structure, the CFTC reached for the narrower, more familiar device of the no-action letter, extended by class rather than rewritten as a rule. That's a smaller ask institutionally, but it produces a similar practical result: an entire category of firms gets a green light to operate without registering, while the underlying registration requirement stays on the books untouched. Neither agency has closed the legislative gap the CLARITY Act would have closed, but both have found administrative paths around it instead.


## Conditions Instead of Caps


The SEC's order caps its sandbox with hard numbers: symbol counts, a percentage of average daily volume. The CFTC's letter skips numeric limits and relies on conduct instead: no statutory disqualification, disclosures to users, joint-and-several liability with each "Registrant," NFA-consistent marketing, recordkeeping, and a notice filing with MPD. In exchange, passive software providers, or PSPs, can build front-end interfaces, market their Registrant relationships, and steer users toward specific ones, as long as users can still reach those Registrants on their own.


## Custody Is the Line the CFTC Draws


What keeps this from being an open door is the custodial model underneath it. Covered activities require that a user's funds sit with the exchange's clearing organization or with a registered broker, never with the PSP. The PSP itself is barred from holding assets, issuing buy or sell signals, or exercising discretion over order routing or execution. It's a narrower version of the same principle behind the SEC's no-leverage and no-custody conditions for tokenized equity venues: the regulator will tolerate software that gets users to a regulated market, not software that starts to look like the market itself.


## An Interim Position, Not a Rule


Like the SEC's order, the CFTC’s letter is explicit about its own impermanence. It binds only the Division, not the Commission and applies only until a rulemaking addresses IB registration for software developers.The letter can be conditioned, modified, suspended, or revoked at MPD's discretion. Both agencies are governing a market they don't yet have durable rules for, using the most flexible instruments in their respective toolkits, an exemptive order at the SEC, a class no-action letter at the CFTC. Both are careful to frame that interim status as a feature rather than an accident. Congress may not have moved this week, but neither regulator was interested in waiting to see if it eventually would.


## Final Thoughts


Whatever the durability concerns, the practical reality is that this patchwork is what the industry has to work with for now. CLARITY failed (for now), and rather than leave the market structure question open, the SEC and CFTC each reached for the tools already available to them, an exemptive order in one case, an expanded no-action letter in the other, to give firms a way to operate in the meantime.


Neither is a substitute for legislation. Both are revocable at the issuing agency's discretion, and both apply only until a rulemaking or a statute replaces them. The seams between the two regimes, different conditions, different agencies, no visible coordination, are the kind of inefficiency that only a single legislative framework can really smooth out. Firms operating across both tokenized equities and derivatives will have to satisfy two separate sets of conditions with no guarantee they line up.


But that's the trade the industry is making right now: imperfect, overlapping relief today instead of clean rules on some future timeline. Until Congress passes something comprehensive, this is the market structure that exists, and firms will need to build compliance programs that can operate under it, not around it.
